With sd × 1.5 all rules find essentially every change (power at least 99.88%), and the median delay is 47 to 57 steps for e-BH, 51 to 66 for Bonferroni SR and 41 to 42.5 for the naive rule.

**Reading.** e-BH recovers most of what Bonferroni loses as K grows. With 60% of 50 assets changing together, Bonferroni's power falls to 84% and its median delay rises to 174 steps; e-BH stays at 96% and 138 steps (96% and 127 steps at K = 5). The gain is largest when many assets change, which is when the e-BH bar drops furthest. Delays are measured on different sets (e-BH detects a superset of Bonferroni's detections, including harder ones), so the delay comparison, if anything, favours Bonferroni. The naive rule is faster still but, as Q15a shows, gives no multiplicity control.

**Estimated baselines (robustness).** With the confidence-sequence baseline (`docs/math.md`, section 6) estimated from 1,440 null steps per asset, δ = 0.01 split over K (so the proved bound is α + δ = 6%), K = 20, 20% of assets changing together by sd × 1.25, 400 paths (`results/e15a_cs_baseline.csv`):

| Dependence | Rule | P(any false discovery), no change | P(any false discovery), with changes | Power | Median delay |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| factor + co-jumps | e-BH | 0% | 0% | 41.0% | 213 |
| factor + co-jumps | Bonferroni | 0% | 0% | 35.5% | 212.5 |
| independent | e-BH | n/a | 0% | 36.0% | 234 |
| independent | Bonferroni | n/a | 0% | 33.0% | 224.5 |

With the oracle baseline the same designs give 93.3% (e-BH) and 88.8% (Bonferroni) power with a common factor, 94.1% and 88.4% with independent assets. **Negative result:** the provable baseline costs more than half the power at this small change, much more than the multiplicity correction does. The confidence-sequence bounds per asset are at level δ/K = 0.0005, so they are wide.

### Q15c. One guarantee per block against one for the whole horizon [SYNTHETIC]

K = 20 independent assets, ten blocks of 390 steps (3,900 steps). Either no change, or 6 assets change (sd × 1.5) at times drawn uniformly over the whole horizon. Baselines are the exact null mean throughout (no recalibration). 400 paths (`results/e15c_horizon.csv`). The block rules restart every 390 steps and the first discovery of each asset over the ten blocks is kept; the "since start" rules run one block of 3,900 steps.

| Rule | P(any discovery), no change | P(at least one false discovery), 6 change | FDR, 6 change | E[max FDP over the horizon] | E[false discoveries] | Power | Median delay |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| daily blocks, e-BH | 4.75% | 23.5% | 3.81% | 6.44% | 0.27 | 98.1% | 56 |
| daily blocks, Bonferroni | 4.75% | 4.25% | 0.63% | 1.80% | 0.04 | 98.0% | 63 |
| since start, Pareto weights (h = 390), e-BH | 1.75% | 5.75% | 0.86% | 2.26% | 0.06 | 97.4% | 72 |
| since start, window h = 3,900, e-BH | 2.00% | 5.75% | 0.88% | 1.56% | 0.06 | 97.9% | 67 |

Median delay by the time of the change (`results/e15c_delay_by_change_time.csv`; share of changes detected in brackets):

| Change at step | daily e-BH | daily Bonferroni | since start, Pareto | since start, window 3,900 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 to 389 | 62 (100%) | 64 (100%) | 63 (100%) | 74 (100%) |
| 390 to 1,299 | 59 (99.8%) | 65 (99.8%) | 71 (99.8%) | 71 (100%) |
| 1,300 to 2,599 | 54 (99.6%) | 62 (99.9%) | 72 (99.8%) | 65 (99.9%) |
| 2,600 to 3,899 | 53 (94.9%) | 63 (94.5%) | 76 (92.7%) | 64 (94.0%) |

**Reading.** Two lessons, both predicted by the theory note (section 6).

1. *A guarantee per block is not a guarantee for the horizon.* Under no change, ten daily blocks give 4.75% probability of any discovery, well inside the 10 × 5% that per-block control allows. With changes, daily e-BH has a 23.5% chance of at least one false discovery over the horizon, against 4.25% for daily Bonferroni. The reason: in this design baselines are never recalibrated, so a changed asset is discovered again in every later block; each time, e-BH lowers the bar for the other 19 assets, and the null assets get many chances at a low bar. In each block the FDR guarantee holds, but nothing bounds the pooled count over blocks. The pooled FDR here (3.8%) and worst FDP (6.4%) happen to stay moderate; they are not covered by any theorem.
2. *One e-process for the whole horizon keeps a single guarantee and pays with delay.* The Pareto rule keeps the any-false-discovery probability at 1.75% (no change) and 5.75% (with changes) for all 3,900 steps, but its median delay grows from 63 to 76 steps as the change comes later, the log(1/w) cost of Proposition 2 in the theory note. The last row is censored (changes near the end are often not detected in time), so its medians are biased toward short delays. Daily e-BH and the window rule get *faster* for later changes because earlier discoveries stay in the e-BH set and lower the bar; daily Bonferroni has no such effect and is flat.

### Q15d. Five Binance coins [REAL]

**Setup.** BTC, ETH, XRP, SOL and DOGE against USDT, one-minute log returns divided by a past-only intraday volatility profile (`avmonitor.data.intraday_scale`, 20-day look-back). One block per UTC day (1,440 minutes), α = 5% per day, K = 5. At each UTC midnight each coin is calibrated on its previous 1,440 returns: plug-in baseline (as in E6), c = 3, null band b = 0.25 (the E5/E6 primary setting) or b = 0.5 (the other band of the E6 grid). Window weights over 1,440 returns. Periods: Jul to Dec 2025 (the E6 period) and Jan 2024 to Jun 2025 (the E6 out-of-sample period; blocks start on 22 Jan 2024 to leave room for the profile and calibration). No setting was chosen from E15 results (see `docs/iterations/PANEL.md` for when band 0.5 was added).

Four rules on the same e-value paths: sticky e-BH; Bonferroni (first time the e-value reaches K/α = 100); naive (first time it reaches 1/α = 20); and, as a hindsight benchmark, a per-asset constant threshold chosen after the fact so that it makes exactly as many discoveries as e-BH ("rate-matched"). The vectorised e-BH run was checked step by step against an offline e-BH on the first 40 blocks of every run.

**Validation (as in E6).** For each discovery, the robust sd (scaled MAD) of the coin's next 1,440 returns is divided by the calibration scale. An up discovery is "confirmed" if this ratio is above 1, a down discovery if it is below 1. Controls: for each e-BH discovery, 5 random days of the same asset at the same minute of the day.

| Coins, period | Band | Discoveries: e-BH / Bonferroni / naive | e-BH per day (of 5) | Up confirmed (95% CI), n | Control | Down confirmed (95% CI), n | Control |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jul to Dec 2025 (184 days) | 0.25 | 790 / 762 / 810 | 4.29 | 78.0% (74.2 to 81.4), 500 | 50.4% | 86.4% (81.9 to 89.9), 286 | 48.7% |
| Jan 2024 to Jun 2025 (526 days) | 0.25 | 2,296 / 2,211 / 2,346 | 4.37 | 80.0% (77.8 to 82.1), 1,313 | 46.2% | 84.9% (82.5 to 87.0), 978 | 52.7% |
| Jul to Dec 2025 | 0.5 | 552 / 508 / 573 | 3.00 | 80.7% (76.6 to 84.1), 424 | 49.4% | 96.9% (92.2 to 98.8), 127 | 50.0% |
| Jan 2024 to Jun 2025 | 0.5 | 1,527 / 1,446 / 1,614 | 2.90 | 82.6% (80.3 to 84.6), 1,176 | 47.0% | 96.2% (93.7 to 97.8), 346 | 55.4% |

What e-BH adds over Bonferroni, and what the naive rule adds over e-BH (`results/e15d_validation.csv`, `results/e15d_structure.csv`):

| Coins, period | Band | e-BH only (not Bonferroni): n; up confirmed; down confirmed | naive only (not e-BH): n; up; down | Median / mean minutes e-BH before Bonferroni | e-BH strictly earlier | e-BH discoveries with e-value below K/α |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jul to Dec 2025 | 0.25 | 28; 12 of 21; 5 of 7 | 20; 4 of 10; 9 of 10 | 4 / 32 | 76.8% | 613 of 790 |
| Jan 2024 to Jun 2025 | 0.25 | 85; 20 of 39; 35 of 46 | 50; 10 of 28; 19 of 22 | 4 / 38 | 76.1% | 1,767 of 2,296 |
| Jul to Dec 2025 | 0.5 | 44; 15 of 30; 14 of 14 | 21; 10 of 13; 7 of 8 | 2 / 30 | 71.7% | 408 of 552 |
| Jan 2024 to Jun 2025 | 0.5 | 81; 22 of 52; 29 of 29 | 87; 33 of 58; 25 of 29 | 2 / 24 | 70.5% | 1,101 of 1,527 |

"Strictly earlier" is the share of coin-days found by both rules on which e-BH flagged first. The rate-matched hindsight threshold confirms at the same rate as e-BH in all 12 panel, period, band and direction cells (two-proportion tests, p-values 0.56 to 1.00, `results/e15d_rate_matched_tests.csv`).

**Reading.**

1. *The strict daily null is false on most coin-days.* At band 0.25 e-BH discovers 86% to 87% of coin-days, at band 0.5 58% to 60%, and at band 0.25 there are at least two discoveries on 170 of 184 days. This repeats E9 and E10: under volatility clustering, "the truncated variance stays within 25% of yesterday's level all day" is rarely true for crypto. The FDR guarantee is then nearly empty in practice, because almost every hypothesis is false.
2. *The multiplicity rule changes the timing more than the set.* e-BH finds only 3.7% to 8.7% more coin-days than Bonferroni. But on the coin-days both find, e-BH flags first 71% to 77% of the time, by a median of 2 to 4 minutes and a mean of 24 to 38 minutes (the mean is pulled up by a long tail, see `results/figures/e15_real_discoveries.png`, panel c). 72% to 78% of e-BH discoveries were made while the e-value was still below the Bonferroni level K/α.
3. *Discoveries point the right way.* An e-BH up discovery is followed by a higher robust volatility over the next day 78% to 83% of the time, against 46% to 50% at matched random times; a down discovery by a lower one 85% to 97% of the time, against 49% to 55%.
4. *The marginal up discoveries are weak.* The up discoveries that only e-BH makes (not Bonferroni) are confirmed 42% to 57% of the time, which is near the control rate; marginal down discoveries are confirmed 71% to 100% of the time (small n). The naive rule's extra discoveries are similar. So the extra discoveries add little information beyond what Bonferroni finds; the value of e-BH here is earlier alarms, not more alarms.
5. *e-BH is not better than a well chosen fixed threshold, in hindsight.* A per-asset threshold set after the fact to make as many discoveries confirms at the same rate. The difference is that e-BH's level is fixed in advance and carries the FDR guarantee; the rate-matched threshold (33 to 48 on the e-value scale) was read off the data.

### Q15e. Five coins and the Nifty 50 index on one clock [REAL]

**Setup.** The five coins plus the Nifty 50 index, Feb 2024 to Dec 2025 (700 UTC days, 472 Nifty sessions), K = 6, other settings as in Q15d. Nifty: regular sessions only, 09:15 to 15:30 IST (03:45 to 10:00 UTC), 374 one-minute returns per session; returns divided by a strictly past-only session profile (per-minute median of |r| over the previous 20 sessions, 5-minute smoothing within the session, normalised to median 1; E7's settings without its start-up look-ahead). Outside its session the Nifty return is missing: its e-process does not move and its clock does not advance. Nifty has its own clock throughout: window h = 374 returns (one session), calibration on its previous 750 returns (E7's primary setting). Each UTC day contains at most one Nifty session. Nifty stays in the panel on weekends and holidays with e-value 1, so K = 6 every day (a small, conservative cost).

Panel totals (`results/e15d_validation.csv`):

| Band | Discoveries: e-BH / Bonferroni / naive | e-BH per day (of 6) | Up confirmed (95% CI), n | Control | Down confirmed (95% CI), n | Control | Median / mean minutes e-BH before Bonferroni |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.25 | 3,257 / 3,107 / 3,352 | 4.65 | 80.8% (79.0 to 82.5), 1,906 | 47.2% | 85.7% (83.7 to 87.4), 1,347 | 52.3% | 5 / 35 |
| 0.5 | 2,120 / 1,990 / 2,273 | 3.03 | 82.8% (80.9 to 84.6), 1,638 | 48.0% | 95.8% (93.7 to 97.3), 481 | 53.1% | 2 / 25 |

Nifty discoveries only (`results/e15e_nifty_discoveries.csv`; controls are pooled over assets in this design and are not reported separately for Nifty):

| Band | Rule | Up confirmed, n | Down confirmed, n | Discovered outside the Nifty session |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.25 | e-BH | 92.1% (116 of 126) | 87.0% (87 of 100) | 3 up, 1 down |
| 0.25 | Bonferroni | 91.0% (101 of 111) | 88.1% (74 of 84) | 0 |
| 0.25 | naive | 89.7% (122 of 136) | 89.4% (93 of 104) | 0 |
| 0.5 | e-BH | 90.4% (75 of 83) | 95.2% (20 of 21) | 1 up |
| 0.5 | Bonferroni | 89.7% (70 of 78) | 100% (16 of 16) | 0 |
| 0.5 | naive | 92.3% (84 of 91) | 83.3% (25 of 30) | 0 |

e-BH discovered Nifty on 226 of 472 sessions at band 0.25 (48%) and 104 at band 0.5 (22%). Which assets are discovered together on a day (`results/e15e_codiscoveries.csv`): at band 0.25, all six on 144 days and all five coins without Nifty on 329 of 700 days; Nifty alone on 4 days. At band 0.5: all six on 35 days, the five coins without Nifty on 212, Nifty alone on 28.

**Reading.**

1. *Trading hours are handled without any synchronisation.* Each asset runs on its own clock and its own calibration window, and the guarantee needs only that the trading calendar is known one step ahead. The Nifty discoveries confirm at about 87% to 95% in both directions.
2. *Borrowing strength across assets is real and visible.* Under e-BH, Nifty was discovered 4 times (band 0.25) and once (band 0.5) after its session had closed: its e-process was frozen, but crypto discoveries later in the UTC day lowered the e-BH bar below Nifty's frozen e-value. Bonferroni and naive rules cannot do this by construction. Such a discovery means "Nifty's session already looked different, and the market-wide picture makes it count" (`docs/theory_panel.md`, section 7).
3. *The coins move together, Nifty much less.* At band 0.25 the five coins are discovered together on 329 of 700 days without Nifty and on 144 more with it. At band 0.5 Nifty is discovered alone on 28 days, as often as XRP and more often than any other coin. Crypto and Indian equity volatility regimes overlap only partly.

### Caveats

* **Oracle baselines in Q15a to Q15c.** The synthetic validity results use the exact null mean. With the confidence-sequence baseline (proved bound α + δ) power falls from about 93% to 36% to 41% in the one design tested; with the plug-in baseline used on real data there is no proved bound (E4d, E8).
* **The real-data null.** The strict daily null with a band is false on most crypto days (point 1 of Q15d). A forecast-relative null (E10) would make the panel's discoveries mean "the forecast was wrong", which is closer to what a user wants; this was not tested in the panel.
* **Which past the null conditions on.** Theorem 1 needs each asset's null to hold given the whole panel's past. If volatility spills over from one asset to another with a lag, this is stronger than the asset's own-past null. E15 does not test for spillovers.
* **Validation is a proxy.** "Confirmed" compares the next day's robust volatility with the calibration scale. It measures persistence of the regime, not whether the null was false at the discovery time, and the controls are pooled over assets.
* **Nifty data cleaning.** E7 sets frozen-price runs (5 or more minutes of exact zero returns) to missing. E15 did not apply that filter, but E7's list of such runs (`results/e07a_frozen_runs.csv`) has none in 2024 or 2025, so it would not have changed the input.
* **Per-block guarantee only.** Q15c shows that per-block FDR control does not bound false discoveries pooled over many blocks.
* **Seeds and sample sizes.** Synthetic rows use 600 paths (2,000 under no change), so a power estimate near 90% has a standard error of at most about 1.2 points (one changed asset); differences between e-BH and Bonferroni of 2 points or less at K = 5 or 10 are within noise.

The alternatives are kept apart from the main package in `alternatives/<name>/`, each with its own README (problem, mathematics, implementation, methodology, limitations), results and tests. `alternatives/ALTERNATIVES.md` ranks them. The sections below summarise each one.

## Report part ALT1: two alternative prototypes

Scripts, tests, READMEs and full results are in `alternatives/quarticity_stream/` (A3) and `alternatives/preaveraging/` (A1). Every number below is copied from the `results/` folders of those prototypes. [SYNTHETIC] marks simulated data, [REAL] marks Binance spot one-minute bars (1 July to 31 December 2025).

## A3. Monitoring quarticity itself: the e-detector on `min(r^4, tau^4)`

**Question.** The main monitor bets on the truncated squared return. The same bets on the truncated fourth power `Q_t = min(r^4, tau^4)` target the truncated local quarticity of Bapat (2026). Is that valid, how does it compare on pure variance changes, does it see changes of shape (tails, vol of vol) that the variance stream cannot, and what do its alarms mean on real data?

**Method.** Two things had to be derived: the null mean `q0` (the model-free sample mean of `min(r^4, tau^4)` over the calibration window; the Gaussian shortcut `3 m0^2` is 2.7% too high at `c = 3` and 21% too high with the raw MAD) and the decrease bet range `lambda < 1 / (tau^4 / q0 - 1) = 0.037` for normal returns, against 0.124 for the variance stream. With those, the proofs of `docs/math.md` section 5 apply unchanged. Settings as in E4: `tau = 3 x scaled MAD` from a 2000-step calibration window, `A = 7800`, 300 paths. A theory function computes the mean shift and signal-to-noise ratio of each stream under any alternative density.

**Q1 Validity [SYNTHETIC].** No change, 20,000 steps. False alarm within 390 steps (bound 5%) and censored mean run length (bound 7800): Gaussian 1.7% / 9471 (up) and 0.0% / 9046 (down); jumps 1.7% / 9348 and 0.0% / 9334; Student t5 2.7% / 8858 and 0.0% / 8558. Both bounds hold in every cell, for both streams.

**Q2 Pure variance change [SYNTHETIC].** Median delay in steps, Gaussian returns (jumps in brackets):

| sd ratio | x 1.25 | x 1.5 | x 2 | x 0.8 | x 0.67 | x 0.5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| variance stream | 96 (92) | 38 (40) | 18 (18) | 153 (151) | 95 (99) | 68.5 (74) |
| quarticity stream | 87.5 (91) | 33 (37) | 13 (14) | 271 (299) | 201.5 (216) | 168 (189) |

**Q3 Shape changed, variance fixed [SYNTHETIC].** 20,000 steps after the change, `A = 400,000` (null false alarm within the horizon at most 5%), 200 paths. Share detected (median delay):

| Alternative | variance stream, up | variance stream, down | quarticity stream, up |
|---|---|---|---|
| Student t3 / t5 / t8 | 0% / 0% / 3% | 100% (650) / 96.5% (3937) / 57.5% (8448) | 6% / 71.5% (6461) / 75% (7626) |
| two-point mixture, d = 0.5 / 0.7 / 0.9 | 8% / 5% / 2% | 28% / 46% / 58% | 82.5% (4915) / 99.5% (2678) / 99% (1033) |
| slow SV, log-sd 0.3 / 0.5 | 100% (715) / 100% (496) | 100% (524) / 100% (271) | 100% (664) / 100% (442) |

**Q4 Real data [REAL].** `A = 28,800` per side, 1440-minute calibration, recalibration after each alarm, band 0.25. Alarms per day: variance monitor 0.69 (BTC) and 0.69 (DOGE); quarticity monitor 0.71 and 0.70. Share of quarticity alarms on the same UTC day as a variance alarm: 87% and 87%; within one hour: 62% and 60%. Median truncated variance in the next 24 hours over the baseline: 1.45 and 1.38 after up alarms, 0.59 and 0.66 after down alarms (control at random times: 1.00). The 34 to 35 quarticity alarms per coin that are more than four hours from any variance alarm are still followed by a move in the flagged direction 80% and 88% of the time. All monitors on both coins alarmed at 15:28 to 15:31 UTC on 10 October 2025, the crypto crash after the US tariff announcement (checked online, `results/q4_real_event_check.csv`). With the same variance tolerance (band 0.5625 on quarticity), the quarticity monitor alarms 20% less often and its decrease alarms are followed by lower variance 100% and 97% of the time.

**Reading.**
* Valid, as the theory says.
* On pure variance changes the quarticity stream is 1% to 28% *faster* for increases (the fourth power amplifies the shift more than it adds noise) and 1.8 to 2.6 times slower for decreases (the bet cap).
* It detects vol-of-vol changes at fixed variance that the variance stream cannot (82% to 99% against 2% to 8%), but it does *not* beat the variance stream on fat tails at `c = 3`: clipping at 3 sd removes most of a fat tail's fourth moment, while the extra mass near zero lowers the truncated variance, so a Student t registers on the variance stream as a volatility *decrease*. At `c = 5` the theory reverses the ranking. The clipping level decides which shape changes are visible.
* On real data the two monitors behave alike; no pure shape event was found in six months of two coins. A planned shape diagnostic (`q_ratio / var_ratio^2`) measured only the mechanics of a fixed `tau` and is reported as such.

**Caveats.** Shape detection needs thousands of steps (signal-to-noise 0.03 to 0.10 per step). A first version of Q3 with `A = 7800` was unreadable because the null itself alarms within 10,000 steps on half the paths; the fix is recorded in `docs/iterations/ALT1.md`.

## A1. Pre-averaging before MAD truncation: microstructure noise at one-second sampling

**Question.** Under the standard price-noise model, at what noise-to-signal ratio `gamma = omega / (sigma sqrt(delta))` does the plain truncated estimator break, for integrated quarticity and for the monitor's local variance, and does pre-averaging (Jacod, Li, Mykland, Podolskij and Vetter 2009) followed by truncation fix it? What happens to the monitor's false alarm rate under noise, with and without pre-averaging, given that pre-averaged returns overlap?

**Method [SYNTHETIC].** One-second returns, 23,400 per day, daily volatility 1%, log-OU stochastic volatility, optional 4 jumps per day of 50 per-second sd, noise sd `gamma` times the per-second return sd. Pre-averaging window `k = 60`, weight `min(x, 1 - x)`; the local pre-averaged variance `V_i = rbar_i^2 / (k psi2 delta)` has mean `sigma^2 + c` with `c = omega^2 psi1 / (psi2 k^2 delta)`, and the local quarticity is corrected as `Q_i = rbar_i^4 / (3 (k psi2 delta)^2) - 2 c V_i + c^2`, whose mean is `sigma^4`; `omega^2` is minus the first autocovariance of clipped raw returns. Truncation of `rbar` at `3 x scaled MAD` by clipping (the paper's rule) or dropping, each with its Gaussian survival factors. Monitors run at `A = steps per day / 0.05`.

**Q1 Integrated quarticity, mean ratio to the truth (relative RMSE) [SYNTHETIC].**

| gamma | 0 | 0.25 | 0.5 | 1 | 2 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| raw returns, MAD clip, no jumps | 0.99 (0.02) | 1.26 (0.26) | 2.23 (1.24) | 9.0 (8.1) | 81.4 (81.5) | 1138 (1155) |
| pre-averaged, MAD clip, no jumps | 0.99 (0.11) | 1.00 (0.11) | 1.00 (0.12) | 0.99 (0.10) | 0.99 (0.11) | 0.99 (0.11) |
| pre-averaged, MAD clip, no noise correction | 0.99 (0.11) | 1.00 (0.11) | 1.00 (0.12) | 1.00 (0.10) | 1.01 (0.12) | 1.10 (0.15) |
| pre-averaged, MAD clip, 4 jumps | 1.14 (0.22) | 1.15 (0.22) | 1.14 (0.20) | 1.17 (0.22) | 1.18 (0.25) | 1.15 (0.24) |
| pre-averaged, MAD drop, 4 jumps | 0.99 (0.12) | 1.00 (0.13) | 1.00 (0.11) | 1.01 (0.12) | 1.02 (0.12) | 0.99 (0.12) |
| pre-averaged, no truncation, 4 jumps | 33.4 (69) | 36.5 (68) | 27.0 (47) | 35.1 (63) | 39.3 (71) | 32.5 (52) |

The raw estimator follows `(1 + 2 gamma^2)^2` exactly: 10% bias at `gamma = 0.16`, a factor 2 at 0.45. Integrated variance follows `1 + 2 gamma^2` (10% at 0.22). The monitor's 300-second local variance on raw returns is inflated by the same `1 + 2 gamma^2` (1.51 at `gamma = 0.5`, 3.07 at 1), while the pre-averaged local variance has mean ratio 0.98 to 1.07 at every noise level but a typical error of 32% (overlapping) to 45% (blocks) against 6% for raw returns without noise.

**Q3 One-day false alarm rate of the monitor, increase side (bound 5%) [SYNTHETIC].**

| gamma | 0 | 0.5 | 1 | 2 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| raw returns (23,400 steps) | 5.0% | 8.5% | **18.0%** | **31.0%** | **41.5%** |
| overlapping pre-averaged, k = 60 | **100%** | **100%** | **100%** | **100%** | **100%** |
| non-overlapping blocks, k = 60 / 20 / 10 | 2.5% / 4.5% / 5.5% | 1.5% / 3.0% / 5.0% | 2.5% / 2.5% / 5.5% | 2.0% / 5.5% / 2.5% | 4.0% / 3.0% / 3.0% |

**Q4 Median detection delay in seconds, sd doubles at the start of the day [SYNTHETIC].** Raw returns 32, 43.5, 86.5, 449.5, 2907 at `gamma = 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4`; blocks with `k = 10`: 259, 269, 299, 359, 649; `k = 60`: 1319 to 1379 throughout. For a halving at `gamma = 4` the raw monitor detects on 70% of days (median 10,795 s); the `k = 10` blocks on 100% (3939 s).

**Reading.**
* Truncation alone does nothing against noise; the plain estimator is off by 26% at `gamma = 0.25` and useless by `gamma = 1`. Pre-averaging then truncation is unbiased at every noise level, at the cost of a relative RMSE of 0.11 instead of 0.02 when there is no noise. Switch it on when the estimated `gamma` exceeds about 0.15.
* After pre-averaging, clip must become drop: a clipped jump keeps `tau^4` in each of the `k - 1` windows it enters (+12% to +18% with 4 jumps per day, growing with `k`).
* Overlapping pre-averaged returns break the e-detector completely: the conditional-mean null fails because consecutive windows share `k - 2` returns. Blocks on disjoint prices restore it at every `k`.
* **The raw-return monitor also loses its guarantee under price noise** (8.5% at `gamma = 0.5`, 41.5% at 4). With price noise `E[r_t^2 | past] = sigma^2 delta + omega^2 + E[u_{t-1}^2 | past]`, so squared returns are positively autocorrelated and the conditional null fails. E4 of the main report saw 3.7% at `gamma = 0.5` only because it looked at 390 steps. The remark in `docs/math.md` 5.1 that the null allows any dependence should be qualified: only dependence that keeps the *conditional* moment on the null side.
* The practical monitor at one second is the `k = 10` block monitor: valid at every noise level, 8 times slower than raw returns without noise, faster than them (and valid, which they are not) from `gamma` of about 2.

**Caveats.** Constant volatility in Q3 and Q4 (so the noise effect is isolated); i.i.d. Gaussian noise, which real noise is not (Hansen and Lunde 2006); the fourth-moment correction assumes local Gaussianity of the pre-averaged return; no real one-second data was available in this environment.

## A1 follow-up (B69). Noise and jumps together, the published benchmark, and the block monitor's guarantee

**Question.** When microstructure noise and jumps are present at the same time, how does pre-averaging then MAD truncation compare with the estimator built for exactly that case, the modulated bipower and multipower variation of Podolskij and Vetter (2009, *Bernoulli* 15(3), 634 to 658), for integrated quarticity and variance? And for the monitor: what exactly is the guarantee of the non-overlapping block version under price noise, and how should the block size `k` be chosen?

**Method [SYNTHETIC].** `alternatives/preaveraging/run_benchmark.py` (two processes, about 2 minutes). Q5: one-second returns, 23,400 per day, log-OU stochastic volatility, 200 paths per cell, noise ratio `gamma` in `{0, 0.5, 1, 2}` x jumps per day and size in `{none, 2 x 25 sd, 2 x 100 sd, 8 x 25 sd, 8 x 100 sd}` (25 per-second sd is 0.16% of the price). Estimators: raw MAD clip (Bapat 2026); pre-averaged (`k = 60`) MAD drop (ours) and MAD clip; modulated bipower (variance) and tripower (quarticity) variation with `K = 76`-step increments averaged over 152 blocks of 153 observations (`c1 = 0.5`, `c2 = 1`), noise-corrected through the exact block weights; pre-averaged bipower and tripower; pre-averaged without truncation. Q6: constant volatility, `gamma` in `{0.5, 1, 2, 4}`, blocks `k` in `{4, 6, 10, 14, 20, 30, 60}`, `A = (n / k) / 0.05`, sd `x 2`, `x 1.5` and no change, 200 paths per cell.

**Reference check.** Title, authors, journal, volume and pages of Podolskij and Vetter (2009) and the arXiv listing 0909.0827 were confirmed from search listings; the full text could not be fetched (arxiv.org, projecteuclid.org, repec.econ.au.dk and eldorado.tu-dortmund.de are blocked here). The block-average variance constants `nu1 = c1^2 (3 c2 - 4 c1) / (3 (c2 - c1)^2)` and `nu2 = 2 c1 / (c2 - c1)^2`, and the CLT standard error from the independent Gaussian block approximation, are therefore our own derivation, verified by simulation in the tests; no equation numbers are quoted.

**The negative finding, in one table. One-day false alarm rate of the monitor under price noise, bound 5%, 200 days per cell [SYNTHETIC].**

| monitor (steps per day, `A`) | side | gamma = 0 | 0.5 | 1 | 2 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| raw truncated returns (23,400, 468,000) | up | 5.0% | **8.5%** | **18.0%** | **31.0%** | **41.5%** |
| raw truncated returns | down | 7.5% | **9.0%** | **13.5%** | **29.0%** | **27.5%** |
| overlapping pre-averaged, k = 60 (23,341, 466,820) | up and down | **100%** | **100%** | **100%** | **100%** | **100%** |
| non-overlapping blocks, k = 60 (390, 7800) | up | 2.5% | 1.5% | 2.5% | 2.0% | 4.0% |
| non-overlapping blocks, k = 60 | down | 0.0% | 0.5% | 1.0% | 2.0% | 1.5% |
| non-overlapping blocks, k = 20 (1170, 23,400) | up | 4.5% | 3.0% | 2.5% | 5.5% | 3.0% |
| non-overlapping blocks, k = 20 | down | 3.0% | 5.0% | 1.0% | 3.5% | 2.5% |
| non-overlapping blocks, k = 10 (2340, 46,800) | up | 5.5% | 5.0% | 5.5% | 2.5% | 3.0% |
| non-overlapping blocks, k = 10 | down | 1.5% | 4.0% | 2.0% | 2.0% | 4.5% |
| non-overlapping blocks, k = 4 (5850, 117,000), Q6 | up | n/a | 4.5% | 4.5% | 3.5% | 4.5% |

Monte Carlo sd of each entry is about 1.5 points at a true 5%. The raw-return monitor's rate rises monotonically with `gamma` on both sides; the block monitors stay within the bound in all 58 cells (28 of Q6, 30 of Q3, with the four entries above 5% within 1.5 points of it).

**Why: the conditional null under MA(1) noise, and what blocks restore.** With observed prices `Y_j = X_j + u_j` (noise i.i.d., mean zero, variance `omega^2`, any distribution) the raw return is `r_t = Delta X_t + u_t - u_{t-1}` and, with `F_{t-1}` containing `Y_{t-1}`, `E[r_t^2 | F_{t-1}] = sigma^2 delta + omega^2 + E[u_{t-1}^2 | F_{t-1}]`. The last term has mean `omega^2` but is not constant (for Gaussian noise and the previous return alone, `E[r_t^2 | r_{t-1}] = sigma^2 delta + 2 omega^2 + rho_u^2 (r_{t-1}^2 - sigma^2 delta - 2 omega^2)` with `rho_u = gamma^2 / (1 + 2 gamma^2)`), so after a large squared return the conditional mean exceeds the baseline with no change in volatility: the null `E[Y_t | F_{t-1}] <= 1` of the e-detector fails, and so does the bound. The block monitor uses `Z_b = min(rbar_b^2, tau^2)` with `rbar_b` pre-averaged over the prices `Y_{bk}, ..., Y_{bk+k-1}`; the return between `Y_{bk+k-1}` and `Y_{(b+1)k}` is skipped, so block `b+1` shares no price with block `b`, its noise values are fresh, and given everything up to the end of block `b` it has the law of a pre-averaged return of a process started there. The independence is exact, not up to a boundary term (if adjacent blocks shared one price the shared noise value would give `Cov(rbar_b, rbar_{b+1}) = -omega^2 / k^2`, an `O(1/k)` relative dependence against the noise part `omega^2 / k`; skipping one return removes it). The null `H0: E[Z_{b+1} | G_b] <= m0`, with `m0` the calibration mean that includes the noise term `psi1 omega^2 / k`, then holds whenever the spot variance over block `b+1` is at most its calibration value and the noise and jump laws are unchanged, by monotonicity of `min(s^2 e^2, tau^2)` in `s`. The betting factor `1 + lambda (Z_{b+1} / m0 - 1)` with a predictable `lambda in [0, 1)` has conditional mean at most 1, so the Shiryaev-Roberts statistic over blocks is an e-detector with respect to the block filtration and Theorems A and B of `docs/math.md` apply with `m = floor(n / k)` blocks per day and `A = m / 0.05`. Nothing requires Gaussian blocks, so the guarantee holds for every `k >= 2`, which Q6 confirms down to `k = 4`. Full statement in `alternatives/preaveraging/README.md`, section 2.

**Q5 Integrated quarticity with noise and jumps, mean ratio to the truth (relative RMSE) [SYNTHETIC].**

| cell | raw, MAD clip | pre-averaged, MAD drop (ours) | modulated tripower (PV 2009) | pre-averaged tripower |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| no jumps, gamma = 0 / 1 / 2 | 0.99 (0.02) / 8.9 (8.0) / 81 (81) | 0.98 (0.11) / 0.98 (0.11) / 0.98 (0.11) | 1.00 (0.30) / 0.99 (0.33) / 1.00 (0.30) | 1.00 (0.13) / 1.00 (0.13) / 1.00 (0.12) |
| 2 x 25 sd, gamma = 0 / 1 | 0.99 (0.02) / 9.0 (8.1) | 0.99 (0.10) / 0.98 (0.11) | 1.12 (0.37) / 1.03 (0.34) | 1.06 (0.15) / 1.04 (0.16) |
| 2 x 100 sd, gamma = 0 / 1 | 0.99 (0.02) / 9.1 (8.2) | 0.99 (0.12) / 0.98 (0.11) | 1.63 (1.27) / 1.57 (1.73) | 1.45 (0.86) / 1.56 (1.63) |
| 8 x 25 sd, gamma = 0 / 1 | 1.00 (0.02) / 9.1 (8.2) | 1.02 (0.11) / 1.05 (0.12) | 1.27 (0.57) / 1.35 (0.65) | 1.21 (0.33) / 1.25 (0.34) |
| 8 x 100 sd, gamma = 0 / 1 / 2 | 1.00 (0.02) / 9.1 (8.1) / 81 (81) | 1.00 (0.11) / 1.01 (0.12) / 1.01 (0.12) | 4.9 (10) / 5.8 (14) / 4.5 (6.9) | 4.0 (7.8) / 3.6 (4.8) / 3.8 (5.2) |

Integrated variance: ours 0.99 to 1.02 (RMSE 0.05 to 0.06) in all 20 cells; modulated bipower 0.99 to 1.01 (0.13 to 0.14) without jumps, 1.05 with `2 x 25 sd`, 1.10 with `8 x 25 sd`, 1.16 to 1.20 with `2 x 100 sd`, 1.72 to 1.83 with `8 x 100 sd`. Coverage of the modulated bipower 95% CLT interval: 0.905 to 0.955 without jumps (half-width 26% of the truth), 0.905 to 0.97 with 25 sd or two 100 sd jumps, 0.57 to 0.62 with `8 x 100 sd`.

**Q6 Median detection delay in seconds for a doubling of the sd, blocks of size `k` [SYNTHETIC].**

| gamma | k = 4 | 6 | 10 | 14 | 20 | 30 | 60 | best observed | `k* = 6 gamma / 2` | rule `max(4, 4 gamma)` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | **127** | 179 | 269 | 370 | 479 | 749 | 1319 | 4 | 1.5 | 4 |
| 1 | **179** | 206 | 289 | 377 | 539 | 719 | 1439 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 2 | 405 | **332** | 354 | 419 | 539 | 764 | 1439 | 6 | 6 | 8 |
| 4 | 2131 | 1154 | 689 | **615** | 659 | 869 | 1439 | 14 | 12 | 16 |

For `x 1.5` the best observed `k` is 4, 4, 10, 20 against `k* = 6 gamma / 1.5` = 2, 4, 8, 16 (delays 299, 459, 839, 1539 s). The delay formula: after a sd change by `v` the block value has mean `(v^2 + rho_k) / (1 + rho_k)` with noise share `rho_k = 12 gamma^2 / k^2`, the bet grows by about `snr^2 / 2` per block with `snr = (v^2 - 1) / (sqrt(2) (v^2 + rho_k))`, so the delay in seconds is proportional to `k (v^2 + rho_k)^2`, minimised at `rho_k = v^2 / 3`, that is `k* = 6 gamma / v`. The curve is flat within 10% for `k` between `k* / 1.5` and `1.5 k*`, so the single rule `k = max(4, ceil(4 gamma))` (target `v = 1.5`, `gamma` estimated from `omega^2 = -mean(r_t r_{t-1})` over `mean(r_t^2) - 2 omega^2`) is within 10% of the best observed delay in all 8 cells.

**Reading.**
* The raw-return monitor's loss of validity under price noise is real, monotone in `gamma` and two-sided; it is not a Monte Carlo artefact (41.5% against 5%). It is the one claim of the main package that one-second data breaks. The fix is not pre-averaging as such (overlapping pre-averaged returns give 100% false alarms) but non-overlapping blocks, whose guarantee is exact for every `k >= 2`.
* Against the published noise-and-jump estimator, pre-averaging then MAD drop is unbiased over the whole grid and 2.5 to 3 times more precise without jumps; the modulated multipower estimators keep `|J|^{4/3}` per affected product at `n = 23,400`, a factor 4.5 to 5.8 in quarticity with eight 0.65% jumps, and its CLT interval then covers 60%. Noise and jumps do not interact for any estimator: pre-averaging handles one, truncation the other, and the two compose.
* The block size is a solved trade-off: `k* = 6 gamma / v`, in practice `k = max(4, 4 gamma)`. At `gamma <= 1` the smallest block (`k = 4`) is best and detects a doubling in 127 to 179 s, a factor 3 to 4 behind the raw monitor's 43.5 to 86.5 s, which is invalid there; the previously reported factor 8 came from `k = 10`.

**Needed changes outside ALT1's files.** `docs/math.md` 5.1 ("the null allows any dependence") and 5.6 should say that MA(1) price noise breaks the conditional null on raw returns and that the block monitor restores it; `ALTERNATIVES.md` A1 can record the benchmark outcome.

**Caveats.** All numbers are synthetic; i.i.d. Gaussian price noise (real noise is autocorrelated and heteroskedastic, Hansen and Lunde 2006); constant volatility in Q6; the delay formula ignores truncation; the modulated bipower constants and interval are our derivation, not the paper's printed ones; no one-second real data was available to estimate actual `gamma` values.

## ALT2. Risk switch: does trading only on the monitor's alarms control risk better than volatility targeting?

Prototype folder: `alternatives/risk_switch/` (README with problem, mathematics, comparison with existing approaches, implementation and methodology; `RESULTS.md` with the full tables; `run_experiment.py`; synthetic tests). Script `alternatives/risk_switch/run_experiment.py`, tables rendered by `summarise.py` into `alternatives/risk_switch/results/summary_tables.md`.

**Question [REAL].** A long position is resized only when the monitor alarms, to `target volatility / (new regime's robust volatility)`, and held until the next alarm. Does this give better risk control than classic EWMA volatility targeting refreshed every minute, hour or day, after transaction costs? Benchmarks: buy and hold, EWMA targeting (Moreira and Muir 2017; Harvey et al. 2018, checked by web search), a daily-refreshed robust rolling estimate (same estimate, no change detection), and the same switch driven by the Gaussian likelihood-ratio monitor.

**Method.** Binance one-minute bars for BTC, ETH, XRP, SOL, DOGE (2024 and 2025) and Nifty 50 one-minute bars (April 2017 to October 2026). Exposure decided at the close of minute t applies to minute t + 1; cost = 5 bp (crypto) or 2.5 bp (Nifty) per unit of turnover, sensitivity 0 to 20 bp. Targets 40% (crypto) and 15% (Nifty) a year, exposure capped at 2. Every setting was chosen on 2024 crypto with a rule stated in advance (lowest tracking RMS among variants whose cost drag is at most 2% a year, mean over the five coins) and then frozen for 2025 crypto and for Nifty. Chosen: EWMA half-lives 3 days (minute and hour refresh) and 1 day (daily refresh); robust rolling 3-day window; switch with 5% false-alarm budget per session, band 0.75, no provisional trade; Gaussian switch with the same settings (over budget, flagged). Metrics: tracking RMS (root mean square of log(weekly realised vol / target)), realised vol, maximum drawdown, worst day, Sharpe with circular block bootstrap 95% intervals (10-day blocks, 2000 draws) and paired differences against daily EWMA, turnover, trades and cost drag.

**Results.** Out of sample, mean of the five coins in 2025 and Nifty 2017 to 2026, base costs.

| Rule | Crypto 2025: tracking RMS | max drawdown | worst day | trades / yr | cost drag | Nifty: tracking RMS | max drawdown | worst day | trades / yr | cost drag | Sharpe diff vs EWMA day, Nifty [95% CI] |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Buy and hold | | -61.0% | -16.9% | 0 | 0 | | -39.3% | -12.7% | 0 | 0 | +0.07 [-0.29, +0.44] |
| EWMA, minute | 0.192 | -40.3% | -13.5% | 525,600 | 1.6% | 0.256 | -28.9% | -4.9% | 92,613 | 0.6% | -0.01 [-0.09, +0.06] |
| EWMA, hour | 0.220 | -39.3% | -9.7% | 8,760 | 1.0% | 0.258 | -28.6% | -4.9% | 1,730 | 0.3% | +0.02 [-0.05, +0.09] |
| EWMA, day | 0.205 | -41.6% | -10.2% | 365 | 1.5% | 0.242 | -30.8% | -5.5% | 246 | 0.4% | reference |
| Robust rolling, day | 0.274 | -43.9% | -9.6% | 362 | 1.6% | 0.291 | -29.0% | -5.7% | 250 | 0.2% | +0.03 [-0.09, +0.14] |
| Switch, robust monitor | 0.271 | -40.9% | -10.6% | 93 | 1.6% | 0.402 | -28.1% | -6.3% | 12 | 0.1% | +0.10 [-0.07, +0.26] |
| Switch, Gaussian LR | 0.242 | -45.9% | -10.6% | 329 | 3.0% | 0.292 | -28.0% | -7.7% | 60 | 0.2% | -0.03 [-0.14, +0.08] |

Alarm rates of the frozen robust monitor: 93 a year per coin on crypto in 2025 (250 with band 0.25), 12 a year on Nifty; the Gaussian monitor 331 and 60. On the equal-weight crypto portfolio the switch's Sharpe difference against daily EWMA is -0.05 [-0.41, +0.32]. In 2020 on Nifty every targeting rule held realised volatility at 16% to 18% against 31% for buy and hold, with worst days of 4.4% to 5.4% against 12.7%.

**Reading.** The switch is a usable risk rule, not a better one. Its tails match EWMA targeting (drawdowns within two percentage points on crypto, smaller on Nifty) with a quarter of the trades on crypto and a twentieth on Nifty, and Sharpe ratios are indistinguishable everywhere. But it is a worse *volatility targeter*: tracking RMS 30% higher on crypto and 65% higher on Nifty, because exposure is frozen between alarms while volatility drifts, and each alarm-driven trade is four times the size of a daily EWMA adjustment, so crypto turnover (31 units a year) equals daily EWMA's despite fewer trades. The expected "matches with fewer trades" holds for trade counts, not for amounts traded. The one clear winner is the trigger: the robust e-detector beats the Gaussian likelihood-ratio monitor, which alarms three to five times as often, costs twice as much to follow and has worse tails on both markets.

**Caveats.** One out-of-sample crypto year (a weak one, so all Sharpe ratios are near zero) and one equity index; a single cost per unit of turnover, no financing or impact; the Nifty backtest is on the index, not futures; the cap of 2 on exposure matters for Nifty in 2026 (a steady decline where levered targeting drew down 18% to 25% against 16% for buy and hold). Full tables, by-coin and by-year breakdowns and the cost grid are in `alternatives/risk_switch/RESULTS.md`.

## Report part ALT3: a robust local plug-in estimator of integrated quarticity (A5)

Code, tests, README (mathematics, proofs, comparison with the literature) and full results are in `alternatives/robust_iq_estimator/`. Every number below is copied from its `results/` folder. [SYNTHETIC] marks simulated data or closed-form theory, [REAL] marks Binance spot one-minute bars (BTCUSDT and DOGEUSDT, 1 July to 31 December 2025, 184 UTC days each). Iteration notes: `docs/iterations/ALT3.md`.

**Question.** Integrated quarticity (`IQ = int sigma^4`, the quantity that sets the width of every confidence interval for daily variance) is estimated in Bapat (2026) by clipping returns at `c x MAD` and averaging kernel-weighted local fourth powers. `docs/estimator_issues.md` lists four problems with it. Can the paper's idea (robust-scale truncation plus local smoothing) be turned into an estimator that is consistent, close to the efficient asymptotic variance `8 int sigma^8`, robust to jumps, equipped with a confidence interval, and better behaved on real minute data?

**Method.** Two changes of principle and one of detail. (1) Aggregate by **squaring a local variance** (the plug-in principle of Jacod and Rosenbaum 2013) instead of averaging local fourth powers: over blocks of k returns, `IQ_hat = sum over blocks of k delta (block mean of r^2 / delta)^2`, whose asymptotic variance is `8 (k + 3) / (k + 2) int sigma^8` (RQ-type estimators, including the paper's averaged kernel, are at `32/3`). (2) Truncate against a **local** scale (median absolute deviation, then a truncated root mean square, over about three blocks) with either a fixed cut-off a = 3 or the growing cut-off `a_n = sqrt(2 log n)`, and **drop** truncated returns rather than clip them. (3) Remove the squaring and truncation biases with an **exact finite-sample correction**, computed from the cumulants of a clipped or dropped squared normal, so the estimator is unbiased under locally constant volatility for every block size. The same algebra gives `int sigma^8` and hence a 95% interval. Main proposal **PI-LU** (local scale, `a_n`, drop, `k = ceil(sqrt n)`). Second proposal **PI-NN** (added in iteration 3, after the real data): PI-LU with the scale raised to 1.4826 times the median of the six nearest absolute returns when that is larger, and blocks of `round(n^(1/4))`. Simulations: log-OU stochastic volatility from `avmonitor.simulate`, vol of vol 0.5 or 1 with a U-shaped intraday pattern, 0 or 4 jumps a day of three sizes, n = 390, 1440, 23,400, 500 days per cell, 15 estimators, true IQ known exactly.

**Q1 Efficiency [SYNTHETIC].** Constant volatility, n = 1440, 8000 days. AVAR in units of `int sigma^8` (closed form / simulated) and efficiency `8 / AVAR`:

| RQ | TPQ | MedRQ | MinRQ | RK-k (Bapat, normalised, corrected) | PI-LU (k = 38) | PI-NN (k = 6) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10.67 / 10.81, 0.74 | 13.65 / 13.48, 0.59 | 14.24 (sim.), 0.56 | 18.50 (sim.), 0.43 | 9.26 (sim.), 0.86 | 8.20 / 8.46, 0.95 | 9.00 / 9.17, 0.87 |

A jump clipped at a = 3 leaves 17.55 (plug-in) or 27.01 (fourth powers) times `sigma^4 delta` (simulation 17.56 and 27.02); a dropped jump leaves 0.003. At n = 390 each clipped jump is 4.5% to 6.9% of the day's IQ.

**Q2 Consistency [SYNTHETIC].** Strong stochastic volatility plus intraday pattern, no jumps (S5): relative bias at n = 390 / 1440 / 23,400 and slope of log RMSE on log n (minus 0.5 is the `sqrt(n)` rate):

| | RK (Bapat) | RK-k | PI-G3 (daily scale) | TRQ-M (Mancini) | MedRQ | PI-LU | PI-NN |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| bias | -0.209 / -0.159 / -0.144 | -0.179 / -0.128 / -0.112 | -0.069 / -0.061 / -0.055 | -0.038 / -0.028 / -0.024 | -0.017 / 0.005 / 0.002 | -0.002 / -0.001 / 0.000 | 0.008 / 0.006 / 0.001 |
| slope | -0.11 | -0.14 | -0.22 | -0.36 | -0.50 | -0.51 | -0.51 |

**Q3 Bandwidth [SYNTHETIC].** The paper's cross-validation (eq. 17 as printed) picks the smallest bandwidth offered (h = 5) on 58% to 97% of days. Its expected value under constant volatility is 74.3, 77.2, 99.2, 142.8 at h = 5, 10, 20, 30 (minimum at h = 5 whatever the data). A corrected target picks the oracle spot bandwidth (median h = 50 to 150), but that oversmooths for the integrated quantity (kernel plug-in RMSE 0.250 at the corrected choice against 0.198 at h = 10, S5, n = 390). The block length of PI-LU matters little in smooth designs (default within 1% to 8% of the best k).

**Q4 Comparison and intervals [SYNTHETIC].** Relative RMSE at n = 390 (n = 1440 in brackets):

**Q5 Real data [REAL].** Median over days of each estimator's ratio to MedRQ of the same day, and rank correlation with MedRQ:

| | RK (Bapat) | RK-k | PI-G3 | TRQ-M | PI-L3 | PI-LU | KPI-L3 | PI-NN | MinRQ | TPQ |

| Spearman, BTC / DOGE | 0.865 / 0.814 | 0.865 / 0.814 | 0.879 / 0.837 | 0.927 / 0.890 | 0.939 / 0.908 | 0.931 / 0.888 | 0.941 / 0.911 | **0.975 / 0.965** | 0.995 / 0.994 | 0.987 / 0.987 |

**Q6 Bursts or jumps [REAL + SYNTHETIC].** Locally standardised one-minute returns: 65% (BTC) and 44% (DOGE) of returns beyond `sqrt(2 log n)` have a neighbour beyond 2 sd, and the lag-1 autocorrelation of capped squared returns is 0.114 and 0.099; isolated jumps on a slowly varying volatility give 0% and minus 0.008. A two-factor volatility model with a fast factor (sd 0.75 in log variance, half-life 3 minutes), picked from a 3 by 3 grid on these diagnostics, gives 41% and 0.120 and reproduces the real ratios (PI-LU / MedRQ 0.68 against 0.66 to 0.69; PI-NN 0.95 against 0.95 to 0.96; 1-minute over 5-minute MedRQ 1.41 against 1.33 to 1.45). In that model, median relative error and RMSE at n = 390 / 1440 / 23,400:

| | RK (Bapat) | PI-LU | MedRQ | TPQ | PI-NN |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| median error, no jumps | -0.58 / -0.59 / -0.57 | -0.49 / -0.47 / -0.26 | -0.40 / -0.20 / -0.02 | -0.40 / -0.20 / -0.02 | -0.36 / -0.23 / -0.04 |
| RMSE, no jumps | 0.59 / 0.59 / 0.59 | 0.49 / 0.46 / 0.27 | 0.42 / 0.29 / 0.08 | 0.42 / 0.28 / 0.08 | **0.39 / 0.28 / 0.07** |
| RMSE, 4 jumps a day | 0.54 / 0.56 / 0.58 | 0.48 / 0.44 / 0.27 | 0.89 / 1.63 / 1.28 | 0.43 / 0.51 / 0.17 | **0.36 / 0.26 / 0.07** |

**Reading.**
* Squaring a local variance instead of averaging fourth powers raises efficiency from 0.74 (RQ, and Bapat's averaged kernel, which is RQ in disguise) to 0.95, and the exact correction makes it unbiased at every n (without it PI-LU is 9.2% too high at n = 390).
* Bapat's rule with one daily MAD is inconsistent when volatility moves during the day: its bias does not shrink (minus 14% at n = 23,400) and its RMSE falls like `n^-0.1`. A local scale restores the `sqrt(n)` rate for every truncation rule; the growing cut-off with dropping (PI-LU) also removes jumps without a residual and is the best estimator in the jump scenarios at n = 390 and 1440.
* The paper's cross-validation choice is a scale artefact, and even a corrected CV answers the wrong question for an integrated quantity: the IQ estimator wants less smoothing than the spot estimator.
* On real data the local estimators agree with MedRQ and MinRQ far better than the MAD-truncated ones, but only PI-NN closes the gap. The diagnosis: large one-minute crypto returns come in bursts of a few minutes, which are part of volatility. In a model calibrated to that, every estimator that truncates against a scale measured over hours (Bapat's, PI-LU, PI-L3, the kernel plug-in) removes 20% to 59% of IQ, while the nearest-neighbour fourth-power estimators keep bursts but break with jumps. PI-NN combines both properties and has the lowest RMSE among robust estimators there, with and without jumps.
* Practical rule: compute the clustering diagnostic first. Isolated large returns: use PI-LU. Clustered ones: use PI-NN, and do not trust agreement with a 5-minute estimate (in the model the 5-minute MedRQ is 0.57 of the true IQ at the median).

**Caveats.** PI-NN was designed after seeing the real data, with settings chosen in exploratory runs (other seeds), so its numbers are not strictly out of sample; it is worse than PI-LU with isolated jumps at small n (S3, n = 390: 0.320 against 0.179) and its `int sigma^8` estimate is not robust. The burst reading is a model fit, not a proof: clustered small jumps or microstructure effects could leave similar signatures, and the daily-scale estimators fit the real data less well (RK 0.53 in the model, 0.33 to 0.42 real). No central limit theorem is proved for the feasible estimators; coverage is numerical evidence. One venue, two coins, six months, no microstructure noise in the simulations.

## ALT4. Can the recipe detect a change in the correlation between two assets, without mistaking a volatility change for it?

Prototype in `alternatives/correlation_monitor/` (README with the formulation and proofs, `RESULTS.md` with every number, Q0 to Q4). Script `run_experiment.py`, results in `alternatives/correlation_monitor/results/`.

**Question.** Bapat (2026) names a multivariate extension as future work. The product of two assets' returns moves when their correlation changes, but also when the volatility of either asset changes or when one of them jumps. Is there a bounded statistic whose conditional mean moves with the correlation only, so that the e-detector of section 5 of `docs/math.md` applies unchanged?

**Method.** Two candidates. (i) The truncated product of standardised returns, `clip(r1 / s1, -c, c) clip(r2 / s2, -c, c)`, bounded in [-c^2, c^2] (the literal "truncated covariance"). (ii) The sign concordance `sign(r1) sign(r2)`, bounded in [-1, 1], with mean `(2 / pi) arcsin(rho)` for any elliptical pair, and invariant to any positive predictable rescaling of either asset (a two-line proof in the README). Both run in the Shiryaev-Roberts betting e-detector with an additive null band, each side at `2A`, so Theorems A and B hold verbatim. Benchmarks: a bivariate Gaussian likelihood ratio e-detector and a Page CUSUM on the raw product tuned to 5% per day under Gaussian pairs.

**Results [SYNTHETIC]** (2000 paths per row, A = 7800, 2000-step calibration, band 0). Share of paths with a false alarm within one day (bound 5%) and within five days (bound 25%):

| Scenario (correlation 0.3 throughout) | sign | product c3 | Gaussian LR | naive CUSUM |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gaussian | 2.9% / 23.0% | 0.0% / 11.3% | 5.0% / 32.0% | 3.2% / 18.4% |
| Student t4 | 2.4% / 23.1% | 0.2% / 15.7% | 79.8% / 100% | 96.2% / 100% |
| Jumps (0.5% per step, 8 sd) | 3.1% / 24.1% | 0.0% / 12.4% | 57.0% / 98.3% | 22.4% / 74.0% |
| Volatility of asset 1 doubles at step 500 | 2.6% / 23.6% | 0.0% / 98.3% (all "up") | 5.1% / 99.9% (97% "down") | 3.8% / 100% |
| Volatility of asset 1 halves at step 500 | 3.1% / 23.8% | 0.0% / 100% (all "down") | 4.6% / 79.6% | 2.7% / 48.2% |
| GARCH(1,1) clustering in each asset (alpha 0.05, beta 0.94), correlation fixed | 2.9% / 23.9% | 2.1% / 63.6% | 25.4% / 83.7% | 33.3% / 87.2% |

Median delay for a correlation change from 0.3 to 0.6 at step 500 (1000 paths): sign 174 steps, product c3 246, product c2 158, Gaussian LR 74 (but 70% to 100% false alarms before the change under t4 or jumps), naive CUSUM 125. For 0.5 to 0.9: sign 65, product c3 194, Gaussian LR 20. A growth-rate calculation predicts these delays within 25% and shows why the product is slow: its bound of 9 caps the admissible bet at 0.11, less than half the growth-optimal bet.

**Results [REAL]** (Binance 5-minute bars, 2024 to 2025, A = 5760 for 5% per day, calibration 5 days, band 0.1). The sign monitor raises 23 to 24 alarms per pair in two years. All 31 increase alarms are followed by a higher Pearson correlation over the next 5 days than in the calibration window (47% to 49% at random times), and 75% to 92% of the decrease alarms by a lower one. Increase alarms follow a negative 24-hour BTC return in 80% of cases and a bottom-decile return in 36% to 50% (10% by construction). The product monitor's decrease alarms coincide with drops in BTC volatility (median after / before ratio 0.83, against 0.99 at random times), the confusion predicted by the simulation; the Gaussian LR raises 4 to 5 times more alarms, 78% to 88% of them "down" and close to chance. At one minute the Epps effect (Pearson 0.02 to 0.06 lower than at 30 minutes) triples the number of "down" alarms, so 5-minute bars are used.

**Basket of four assets [SYNTHETIC and REAL].** The average pairwise sign concordance of k assets is bounded in [-1/(k-1), 1], so one e-detector at level A covers the whole basket with the same guarantee. Against the union of six pairwise monitors at level 6A it is twice as fast for a basket-wide change (72 against 132 steps for all correlations 0.3 to 0.6) and five times slower for a change confined to one pair (451 against 91), and it keeps its bound under t4 and volatility changes (19% to 24% per 5 days against 25%). On BTC, ETH, SOL and DOGE (raw 5-minute returns, band 0.1) it raises 31 alarms in two years; 93% of increase and 94% of decrease alarms are confirmed over the next 5 days (48% at random), and 8 of the 15 increase alarms follow a bottom-decile 24-hour BTC return.

**Reading.** The sign statistic turns the volatility monitor into a correlation monitor with the same guarantee, with no scale estimate and no truncation needed, and it is the only detector tested that a pure volatility change cannot trigger. It pays for this with a delay 2 to 3 times that of the Gaussian-optimal detector on clean Gaussian data, and is about as fast as the truncated product at c = 3, whose bets are throttled by Bapat's truncation bound.

**Caveats.** Plug-in baseline (a band of 0.05 to 0.1 or the confidence-sequence baseline of section 6 is needed; with band 0 the 5-day false alarm rate is 23% against a bound of 25%). The 5-day confirmation on real data can partly reflect mean reversion of the rolling correlation. The basket statistic dilutes a change confined to one pair; weighted variants and a forecast-relative null were not built.

---

## ALT5. Two-sample betting: can the monitor compare the recent window with the calibration window without estimating a baseline?

Code, tests, README (formulation, proof, comparison with the literature) and full results are in `alternatives/two_sample_betting/`. Every number below is copied from its `results/` folder. [SYNTHETIC] marks simulated data, [REAL] marks Binance spot one-minute bars (BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT, 1 July to 31 December 2025, 184 days each). Iteration notes: `docs/iterations/ALT5.md`.

**Question.** The main monitor bets that the mean of the truncated squared return equals a baseline `m0` estimated from the calibration window; its guarantee is proved for a known `m0`. Alternative A4 asks for a sequential two-sample test by betting that detects any change in the law of the returns, with nothing estimated. Is it exactly valid, how much speed does it give up on variance changes, what does it see that a variance monitor cannot, and what does it flag on real data?

**Method.** Each new return is ranked among all earlier returns of the segment (calibration window plus monitored returns, a growing reference), giving a smoothed conformal p-value. Under exchangeability these p-values are exactly i.i.d. uniform (Vovk, Nouretdinov and Gammerman 2003), so any bet `1 + lam (w(p) - b E_U|w|)` with a predictable witness `w` of mean 0 under the uniform law is fair, and the Shiryaev-Roberts mixture of such bets is an e-detector with the guarantees of `docs/math.md` 5.4 (average run length at least `A`, false alarm within `m` steps at most `m / A`), in the filtration of the p-values. The null band `b` allows the density of each p-value to be within `1 +- b` of uniform. Three bettor families: scale up and scale down bets on the Gaussianised truncated score `min(z^2, 9) / kappa2` of the p-value (the main monitor's statistic, but with null mean exactly 1), and histogram learners that estimate the density ratio of new to reference p-values (the rank-space analogue of a kernel two-sample witness, Shekhar and Ramdas 2024). Weights 0.25, 0.25 and 0.5, frozen from a pilot on development seeds. Truncation does not matter for ranks (monotone invariance, ties handled exactly) except to bound the Gaussianised decrease bet. Volatility clustering breaks exchangeability, as it breaks the main monitor's null. `A = 28,800` everywhere (5% per 1440-step day).

**Validity with no change [SYNTHETIC].** 1000 paths per law; share with a false alarm within 1 day (bound 5%) and 7 days (bound 35%), one-day calibration window, and within 1 day with a two-hour window:

| Detector | Gaussian, 1 d / 7 d | Student t4, 1 d / 7 d | Jumps, 1 d / 7 d | Two-hour window, 1 d (three laws) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| main monitor, plug-in, band 0 | 5.4% / **57.0%** | 6.0% / **52.5%** | 4.6% / **51.4%** | **42.0% to 45.7%** |
| rank detector, omnibus, b 0 | 2.4% / 22.6% | 3.1% / 24.2% | 2.4% / 23.0% | 2.2% to 3.5% |
| rank detector, fixed reference (240 / 1440 steps) | 90.4% / 100% and 21.2% / 98.4% (Gaussian, 500 paths) | | | |

The plug-in baseline's error acts as a constant drift that the bets find within days; ranking against the calibration window only (quantile bins learned once) fails the same way, because the p-values then share one reference and are dependent. With the growing reference every rate is below its bound at 1, 7 and 14 days. The repo's proved variant (`baseline="cs"`) is valid but conservative: 0.0% per day and 0.1% per week.

**Power [SYNTHETIC].** Change at monitored step 500, 400 paths, median delay in steps [share detected within 4000 steps when below 95%]:

| Change | main, plug-in, band 0 | main, confidence-sequence baseline | rank, scale bets only | rank, omnibus |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| sd x1.25 | 127 | 348 | 136 | 152 |
| sd x0.8 | 211 | 400 | 222 | 237 |
| Gaussian to t4, same variance | 1203 | 2251 [10%] | 1404 [86%] | **417** |
| jumps 0.2% to 1% per step, same variance | **361** | 1129.5 [92%] | 418 | 399 |
| jumps 0.2% to 0.5% per step, same variance | **1393** [88%] | not run | 1698 [57%] | 1688 [54%] |

The signed score (rank of `u` rather than `|u|`) alone detects a pure skew change (809 steps, 99%); for every `|u|`-based detector the law of the statistic does not change there. Truncating the rank score at 3 sd moves delays by at most about 6%. With a 120-step reference the rank detector stays valid (at most 0.8% false alarms before the change, bound 1.7%) and is 17% to 52% slower; the plug-in monitor with the same window has 11.5% to 14.0%. Under GARCH(1,1) clustering both designs alarm on most days (band 0.25, persistence 0.99: main 67.0%, rank 53.0%).

**Real data [REAL].** Returns divided by `intraday_scale`, one-day calibration, recalibration after each alarm. At band 0.25 the main monitor raises 127 (BTC) and 122 (ETH) alarms, the rank detector 123 and 114; 50% and 61% of the rank alarms are matched by a main-monitor alarm within an hour (chance 5.7%). Each monitor is calibrating about two thirds of the time, and 44 of the 61 unmatched BTC rank alarms (40 of 45 for ETH) fell while the main monitor was calibrating. While the main monitor was watching, the rank detector alone raised 17 BTC and 5 ETH alarms. The BTC ones are shape changes at constant scale: robust scale ratio 0.994, scale-free shape distance 0.131 against 0.076 at random times, and a learned density ratio of 0.32 for the largest 0.2% of moves and about 1.5 for the smallest ones, with more zero returns (5.0% against 3.8% in the reference). Dropping zero returns halves the group to 8, so part of it is a change in price stickiness rather than volatility. The main monitor alone raised 32 alarms per coin while the rank detector watched, all volatility decreases (truncated variance ratio 0.50 and 0.52). With a 120-minute reference the rank detector monitors 88% to 91% of the time.

**Reading.**
* The rank detector has the strongest guarantee of the designs tested: exact for any return law, any reference length and any horizon. The plug-in main monitor holds its bound for a day but not for a week (51% to 57% against 35%), which matters for every deployment that does not recalibrate daily.
* On variance changes it costs 4% to 7% in delay with scale bets alone and 11% to 19% with the full mixture; against the proved confidence-sequence variant it is 1.7 to 2.8 times faster. It is 2.9 times faster than the plug-in monitor for a tail change at fixed variance, which the variance monitors barely see. A change of jump intensity at fixed total variance is a negative result: the variance monitor is faster, because the diffusive variance falls.
* On BTC and ETH the two designs mostly agree; the rank detector adds a few shape alarms and misses some decreases at this band. Its practical gain is the short reference, which the plug-in design cannot use.

**Caveats.** Exchangeability fails on real one-minute returns (clustering), so real alarms are descriptive, not tested discoveries; ranks relative to a volatility forecast are the natural next step and were not built. The bands of the two designs are not on the same scale, so the real-data comparison is between two settings, not two designs in general. The rank detector gives no direction or size for shape alarms beyond the density ratio. About 80 microseconds per step in pure Python against about 10 for the main monitor (`results/t_timing.csv`). The conjecture that the Gaussianised score is asymptotically as efficient as the main monitor under Gaussian data is untested. One venue, two coins, six months.

---

## Limitations and further research

The limitations of all results above are collected in `docs/limitations.md`. The main open directions are: a guarantee that covers persistent volatility clustering without giving up power against structural breaks (E10 shows the trade-off is real); removing the blind period after each alarm (E12, E7); monitoring many assets with a single error guarantee (E15); and noise-robust monitoring on tick data (ALT1).
